course.title: 5 day Cast On | Bind Off | Hem Challenge

components.html:
Quick! How many cast on methods can you name? When would you use each of them?
At the end of this Challenge, you should be able to answer these questions and have a good feel for what cast on to choose for your next project.
I confess, Knit it Now patterns are vague about casting on .... That's by design!
There are so many different cast on methods, not to mention hem treatments, who am I to tell you to "E-wrap cast on" or "chain cast on"?
Let's devote the next few days to exploring the possibilities!

Open Cast on
By definition, an open cast on will have stitches that may unravel if given the chance.
Some machine manuals will give instruction for this type of cast on.
Here are some variations:
  • Open Cast on with a cast on Comb
  • Open Cast on with a wire
  • Open Cast on with Ravel cord
Most knitters graduate beyond these methods pretty quickly.
The most often used open cast on methods are:
  • Scrap and Ravel
  • Using a Cast on Rag
You will use these again and again

Closed Cast on
With a closed cast on, the starting stitches are secure.
These techniques can be categorized:
  • Closed but temporary
    These cast on methods are quick and have their place ... they just wouldn't be appropriate for the finished edge of your next sweater.
    Uses:
    • Cast on for swatching
    • Scrap 'n Ravel Cast on
    • Cut 'n Sew
  • Closed and Functional
    These techniques can be used for the edges of your knitting, without any additional finishing.
    • We'll cover a few of these techniques in the following section

Fast Closed Cast Ons are used when you want to get knitting fast and you will be finishing the edge with another technique.
They are for "your eyes only" and should be considered a raw edge that needs finishing.

components.title: Slip Cast on - Extra FAST! (Brother/Knit King)

components.html:
Fast Closed Cast Ons are used when you want to get knitting fast and you will be finishing the edge with another technique.
They are for "your eyes only" and should be considered a raw edge that needs finishing.

No Weaving Brushes? No Problem!


This is not a video - use the arrows to flip through the images. Turn on the audio for instruction

slides.caption:
Often patterns will instruct you to work a weaving cast on. This is a quick and easy way to get started knitting.
If you don’t have weaving brushes on your machine, you can still work this cast on.
With no brushes, you simply need to weave your cast on yarn manually.
To make the weaving easier, have your needles in working position and then position every other needle as shown. Alternating the positions makes it easier to weave the strand.
Weave yarn over and under, over and under across the row.
Hang a cast on comb to help form those first stitches
You'll notice that there is a single strand of yarn that runs through that first row of stitches
This single strand can be used to quickly gather a knitted piece.

For example, knit a hat from the top down and use the weaving cast on to gather up the top.
Create a flower: Cast on over 6"-8" knit for 1" and then bind off. Pull that cast on yarn strand to gather up the knitting really quickly to form a flower shape and use this to embellish a garment.

components.html:
Slip Cast On
  1. Carriage set for Plain Knitting
  2. Pull out 30 - 60 needles
  3. Align the needles in Working Position
  4. Pull every other needle all the way out (D-E-F)
  5. Set your carriage to slip to the left
  6. Knit left (every other needle will knit)
  7. Hang a cast on comb
  8. Carriage on the left - Cancel Slip
  9. Confirm all stitches are knitting
  10. Continue Knitting
  11. Drop the knitting from the machine or practice binding off
Super Fast Closed Cast on PLUS
  1. Carriage set to Plain Knitting
  2. Pull out 30-60 needles
  3. Put every other needle in out of work position
  4. Hang a cast on comb in the loops
  5. Pull the out of work needles into working position
  6. Continue Knitting
  7. Drop the knitting from the machine or practice binding off
Notice that when you pull on the tail of yarn from the cast on, you can quickly gather up the kntiting. Lots of possibilities with this method! Weaving Cast On For machines with weaving brushes
  1. Carriage set for Plain Knitting
  2. Pull out 30 - 60 needles
  3. Align the needles in Working Position
  4. Pull every other needle all the way out (D-E-F)
  5. Engage both weaving brushes (check your manual)
  6. Carriage on the right
  7. Thread your carriage
  8. Lay the tail of yarn OVER the needles
  9. Hold the tail securely on the left and knit from right to left
  10. Hang a cast on comb and weight
  11. Continue knitting
  12. Drop the knitting from the machine or practice binding off.
Weaving Cast on 2 (without brushes)
  1. Carriage set to Plain Knitting
  2. Pull out 30-60 needles
  3. Put needles into position as shown (to make it easier to weave over and under)
  4. Carriage on the right
  5. Starting on the left, weave the tail of yarn over and under the needles in work.
  6. Hang a cast on comb
  7. Thread the carriage
  8. Knit across the needles in work

Functional Closed Cast Ons can be used as the start of any knitting project. They are closed, secure and pretty enough for public view.
The chain cast on isn't as stretchy as e-wrap, but the chained edge matches a stitch-thru-stitch bind off making the start and finish of scarves and blankets match.
E-wrap cast on is probably the most used method for machine knitters. It can be used for hems and other techniques as well.

Chain Cast On Popular cast on. Firm, not stretchy. Appearance matches a stitch-through-stitch bind off so both ends of a knitted piece match
  1. Carriage set for Plain Knitting
  2. Pull out 30 - 60 needles
  3. Pull every needle all the way out (D-E-F)
  4. Form a slip knot and place it in the hook of your latch tool
  5. Starting on the left (if you are right handed) position the working yarn (from the mast) to the left of the first needle.
  6. Place the tool between the 2 end needles
  7. Reach up and grab the working yarn with the hook of the tool.
  8. Pull down and pull the strand through the loop on the tool
  9. Position the tool between the next 2 needles.
  10. Continue across all needles
  11. Secure the loop on the last needle
  12. Knit Across
It might be difficult to knit across this single chain ... especially if you’ve worked it tightly.
As shown in the video - using waste yarn and weights helps. Try this cast on again when you are familiar with these techniques E-Wrap Cast on (Don't Skip this one!) One of the most popular cast on methods. It’s easy to remember, easy to work, stretchy and has many uses.
  1. Carriage set for Plain Knitting
  2. Pull out 30 - 60 needles
  3. Pull every needle all the way out (D-E-F)
  4. Starting on the left, use the tail of yarn and wrap each needle in a counter-clockwise direction
  5. Keep the loops pushed back against the edge of the machine
It might be difficult to knit across this single cast on edge ... especially if you’ve worked it tightly.
As shown in the video - using waste yarn and weights helps. Try this cast on again when you are familiar with these techniques
Double Strand E-Wrap Cast On
  1. Try the e-wrap cast on with a doubled strand of yarn.
  2. Use a contrasting color of yarn doubled
  3. Using scrap and ravel with weights helps to knit this.
Double E-Wrap Wrap each needle twice, adding stability
  1. Carriage set for Plain Knitting
  2. Pull out 30 - 60 needles
  3. Pull every needle all the way out (D-E-F)
  4. Starting on the left, use the tail of yarn and wrap the first needle in a counter-clockwise direction
  5. Wrap the same needle a second time
  6. Pull the second wrap through the first
  7. Repeat over each needle as needed
  8. Keep the finished cast on stitches near the needlebed
  9. Knit a few inches and drop the work from the machine or practice a bind off technique
Long Tail Cast On
  1. Carriage set for Plain Knitting
  2. Pull out 30 - 60 needles
  3. Pull every needle all the way out (D-E-F)
  4. Starting on the left, use the tail of yarn and wrap the first needle
  5. Keep the strand behind the latch, wrap the 2nd needle
  6. Lay the working yarn over the first needle, positioning it in the hook of the first needle.
  7. Pull the loop in the hook through the loop behind the latch to form your first cast on stitch.
  8. Wrap the 3rd needle
  9. Lay the working yarn over the 2nd needle, positioning it in the hook of the second needle
  10. Pull the loop through, creating the 2nd cast on stitch
  11. Repeat across until all needles are cast on
  12. Knit a few inches and drop the work from the machine or practice a bind off method.

No matter what cast on method you choose, it's recommended that you use the Scrap 'n Ravel technique.
For the Scrap: Use a yarn that is similar in weight to your garment yarn
For the Ravel Cord : Use a strong, smooth yarn in a contrasting color

components.title: Stretchy Bind Off without Gate Pegs

components.html:
Plain or Fancy, hems can add the perfect touch to any knitting project.
If you are knitting a sweater, a simple cast on edge may be the casual look you want. Traditional ribbed hems and cuffs have their place ... but you can do so much more!
No matter what your pattern says, take charge and plan for hems for your next project!

components.title: Hung Hem with Cast on Comb

blocks.title: Break out of the Ribbing Rut

components.html:
Rolled Hem Study
Challenge 1:
Knit 3 swatches with rolled hems, experiment with the tensions as shown in the video
Challenge 2:
Seam two of the swatches, focusing on perfection. Even if this is a quick “cheater’s” hem, there’s no reason for the seam to scream “home-made”.
Basic Hung Hem #1
  1. Cast on 30 - 60 stitches with waste yarn
  2. Knit 6-10 rows
  3. Knit a row of contrasting color ravel cord
  4. Set tension to garment tension MINUS 1
  5. Knit 10 rows
  6. Knit a turning row
  7. Set tension to garment tension
  8. Knit 10 rows
  9. Pick up the open cast on stitches
  10. Make sure you’ve picked up EVERY stitch
  11. Pull out all the needles
  12. Close the latches
  13. Knit a few inches
  14. Drop the work or practice a bind off
  15. Place a ruler or pencil in the hem and pull to “pop” the stitches
Basic Hung Hem #2 (tension change)
  1. Cast on 30 - 60 stitches with waste yarn
  2. Knit 6-10 rows
  3. Knit a row of contrasting color ravel cord
  4. Set tension to garment tension MINUS 2
  5. Knit 10 rows
  6. Knit a turning row
  7. Set tension to garment tension MINUS 1
  8. Knit 10 rows
  9. Pick up the open cast on stitches
  10. Make sure you’ve picked up EVERY stitch
  11. Pull out all the needles
  12. Close the latches
  13. Knit a few inches at GARMENT TENSION
  14. Drop the work or practice a bind off
  15. Place a ruler or pencil in the hem and pull to “pop” the stitches
Basic Hung Hem #3 (e-wrap)
  1. E-wrap Cast on
  2. Set tension to garment tension MINUS 2
  3. Knit 10 rows
  4. Knit a turning row
  5. Set tension to garment tension MINUS 1
  6. Knit 10 rows
  7. Pick up the e-wrap loops
  8. Make sure you’ve picked up EVERY stitch
  9. Pull out all the needles
  10. Close the latches
  11. Knit a few inches at GARMENT TENSION
  12. Drop the work or practice a bind off
  13. Place a ruler or pencil in the hem and pull to “pop” the stitches
Hung Hem Basics #4 (every other needle)
  1. Cast on 30 - 60 stitches over every other needle with waste yarn
  2. Knit a few rows in waste yarn
  3. Knit a row of contrasting color ravel cord
  4. Set tension to garment tension MINUS 2
  5. Change to garment yarn
  6. Knit 4 rows
  7. Pull all needles into working position
  8. Knit 4 rows over all needles
  9. Knit a turning row
  10. Set tension to garment tension MINUS 1
  11. Knit 8 rows
  12. Pick up the open cast on stitches
  13. Make sure you’ve picked up EVERY stitch
  14. Pull out all the needles
  15. Close the latches
  16. Knit a few inches at GARMENT TENSION
  17. Drop the work or practice a bind off
  18. Place a ruler or pencil in the hem and pull to “pop” the stitches

Once you've worked this gorgeous designer hem, you'll never look back! It takes a bit more work, but there is no flair or flipping!
Please, don't just watch the video ... give it a try!

  1. Starting with scrap and ravel cast on 30-60 stitches.
  2. With garment yarn at garment tension knit for 4-6”
  3. Drop the work (or practice a bind off)
  4. With the private (purl) side facing fold the waste yarn back
  5. Reducing the number of stitches by about 15%, rehang the garment stitches on the machine.
  6. Remove the scrap and confirm all stitches are in the hooks
  7. Knit 1 row at garment tension
  8. Knit a marker row*
  9. At garment tension MINUS 1, knit 8-10 rows.
  10. Knit a turning row
  11. At garment tension MINUS 1, knit 8-10 rows
  12. Pick up the marker row
  13. Loosely bind off
  14. Block well.

Picot Bind Off
  1. Carriage on the right
  2. Bind off 2-3 stitches (for easier seaming)
  3. Pull out 3 empty needles
  4. Use your latch tool and pull the working yarn down between the first 2 empty needles
  5. Chain Cast On* 3 stitches by working a chain loosely over the first 2 needles, then hang the loop over the 3rd needle.
  6. Hand knit 5 stitches loosely (including the 3 you just cast on)
  7. Bind off the 5 stitches, stitch-through-stitch and hang the loop on the next needle in work.
  8. The first picot is complete. Repeat across the piece. Binding off the last few stitches without a picot for easier seaming
Chained hem
  1. Cast on with waste yarn and ravel cord.
  2. Using the garment yarn (not in the feeder)
  3. Loosely, Chain Cast On over the ravel cord across the row
  4. For the last stitch, loop the working yarn under the last needle and hang the loop from the latch tool on the last needle.
  5. Push the chain back against the machine
  6. Close the Latches
  7. Free pass* the carriage if needed)
  8. Knit 1 row
  9. Remove the yarn from the carriage and tension mast (to make it easier to chain loosely)
  10. Carefully pull the work away from the needlebed.
  11. Reach under the knitting and chain cast on again, positioning the chain between the knitting and the needlebed. (The chains will present on the knit side of the work)
  12. Free pass the carriage
  13. Repeat steps 3-9 as many times as you like.
Scalloped Eyelet Hem
  1. Cast on over every other needle with waste yarn and ravel cord.
  2. With main yarn, knit 2 rows (every other needle)
  3. Put all needles into working position
  4. Knit 1 row
  5. Hang the very first row of garment yarn on every other needle (small hung hem)
  6. Pull out all needles. Knit 1 row
  7. Transfer every other stitch to create row of eyelets.
  8. Confirm that all needles are in work. knit 1 row
  9. Set carriage to hold in both directions
  10. Pull every 8-10 needle to hold position
  11. Knit 6-8 rows (tucking the needles in hold). Knit slowly and confirm that the needles adjacent to the held needles are knitting
  12. Pull all the needles out
  13. Cancel hold, weight each scallop knit 1 row
  14. Pull the needles out again and knit 1 row
  15. Continue knitting
Scalloped Eyelet Hem -Variation 1
  1. Cast on with waste yarn and ravel cord
  2. E-wrap cast on with double strand
  3. Continue as the Scalloped Eyelet Hem above
Scalloped Eyelet Hem -Variation 2
  1. Use either cast on method (small hem or double e-wrap)
  2. Knit the Scalloped Eyelet Hem
  3. Add a row of eyelets after completing the scalloped tucks

All this talk about casting on and hems ... what about adding a decorative edge AFTER you knit the piece?
Consider decorative afterthought edges.

Now that you have these skills under your belt, let's knit something more than just swatches!
Use the Knit it Now pattern (in the next section) to knit your own Squirrel Cardigan on any machine, with any yarn or stitch pattern!
  • Knit and measure a swatch
  • Choose your size
  • Enter your gauge
  • Build your custom pattern
  • Get knitting!
Are you a brand new knitter?
Knit your Squirrel in plain knitting and concentrate on following the pattern and using your new cast on and bind off skills.
More Experienced?
Knit your Squirrel in a stitch pattern or add stripes. Focus on a new-to-you cast on and bind off method. Experiment with different finishing techniques.
